```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2)
```

This guide is for researchers who validate clinical prediction models and
want to know whether their validation sample is large enough to trust its
conclusion. A validation sample is finite, so the net benefit of a model is
uncertain, and the strategy that looks best (a model, treating everyone, or
treating no one) may not be the best in the population. The
value-of-information (VoI) functions of voipred.dev measure how much that
uncertainty matters for the decision of which strategy to use, following
Sadatsafavi et al. (2023, 2025) for EVPI and EVSI and Wynants et al. (2018)
and Cruz and Korthauer (2025) for the probabilities that a model is useful or
the best. They all take a result of `nb_val()` (see the net benefit guide,
`voipred_nb_guide.Rmd`), with one model or several:

| Function | What it gives |
|---|---|
| `p_useful()` | Probability that each model is better than treating all and treating none |
| `p_best()` | Probability that each strategy (each model, treat all, treat none) is the best |
| `evpi()` | Expected value of perfect information (EVPI) and relative EVPI; also P(useful) and P(best) from the same draws |
| `evsi()` | Expected value of sample information (EVSI) of a future validation study |

Each result has `print()`, `summary()`, `as.data.frame()` and `plot()`, and
EVPI and EVSI can also be drawn below the decision curve. Every function works
for binary, survival and competing-risks outcomes and any number of models.
When models are compared, give them to one call of `nb_val()`, as a list,
and pass that result to the VoI functions; this guide does so throughout,
and its last section shows that results computed separately can be used too.
The help pages give the full details: `?p_useful`, `?p_best`, `?evpi`,
`?evsi`, `?summary.voipred_voi` and the `plot()` methods
(`?plot.voipred_evpi`, ...).

## Installation

voipred.dev is installed from GitHub. plotly (interactive plots) and
patchwork (the panel below a static decision curve) are optional; partykit
and coin are only used for the censoring tree in the EVPI section.
voipred.dev has compiled (C++) code, so installing it needs a C++ compiler:
Rtools on Windows, the Xcode command line tools on macOS
(`xcode-select --install`); Linux has one already.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"),
        install.packages.compile.from.source = "never")
lib <- Sys.getenv("R_LIBS_USER")
dir.create(lib, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
.libPaths(c(lib, .libPaths()))

pkgs <- c(remotes = "0", plotly = "0", patchwork = "0", partykit = "0", coin = "0",
          prodlim = "0", insight = "0", Rcpp = "0", ggplot2 = "3.4.0",
          riskRegression = "2026.3.11")
missing_or_old <- function(p)
  !requireNamespace(p, quietly = TRUE) || utils::packageVersion(p) < pkgs[[p]]
new <- names(pkgs)[vapply(names(pkgs), missing_or_old, logical(1))]
if (length(new)) install.packages(new, lib = lib)

remotes::install_github("amirfarahmand0/voipred_dev", force = TRUE,   # voipred.dev
                        upgrade = "never", lib = lib)
```

Every package this guide uses is checked and loaded here, so that a missing
one is reported at the start rather than halfway through (plotly and
patchwork are only needed for the plots with panels and the interactive
plots):

```{r library}
pkgs <- c("voipred.dev", "survival", "riskRegression", "prodlim", "partykit",
          "coin", "plotly", "patchwork")
missing <- pkgs[!vapply(pkgs, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing))
  stop("Install these packages first (see the code above): ",
       paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
library(voipred.dev)
library(survival)
```

# Setup: the net benefit

**Binary outcome.** GUSTO-I was an international randomized trial of four
thrombolytic strategies in 40,830 patients with acute myocardial infarction
(GUSTO investigators, 1993); voipred.dev ships its data as `gusto`. The
outcome is death within 30 days (`day30`), about 7% of patients. We fit two
logistic models on a random development sample of 5000 patients: a "full"
model (age, Killip class, systolic blood pressure, pulse, previous
infarction, infarct location and sex) and a model with age only. For
illustration, we validate them on a small random sample of only 500 other
patients, the size of the case study of Sadatsafavi et al. (2023), so that
the uncertainty is visible; with thousands of validation patients it would be
small. Both models are given to one call of `nb_val()`:

```{r data-binary}
set.seed(1)
i   <- sample(nrow(gusto))
df_dev_binary <- gusto[i[1:5000], ]
df_val_binary <- gusto[i[5001:5500], ]
fit_full <- glm(day30 ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse + pmi + miloc + sex,
                family = binomial, data = df_dev_binary)
fit_age  <- glm(day30 ~ age, family = binomial, data = df_dev_binary)
df_val_binary$p_full <- predict(fit_full, newdata = df_val_binary, type = "response")
df_val_binary$p_age  <- predict(fit_age, newdata = df_val_binary, type = "response")

z <- seq(0.01, 0.30, by = 0.01)
# both models in one call (a list, one element per model)
res_bin <- nb_val(data = df_val_binary,
                  predicted_risk = list(Full = "p_full", `Age only` = "p_age"),
                  outcome = "day30",
                  thresholds = z)
plot(res_bin)
```

The value-of-information functions take this result and compare all its
models; to analyse a different set of models, call `nb_val()` with those
models.

**Survival and competing risks.** The Rotterdam breast cancer data
(`rotterdam`, from the survival package; Royston and Altman, 2013) describe
2982 women with primary breast cancer. The outcomes are death by 5 years (a
Cox and a Weibull model, compared in one call) and recurrence by 5 years with
death as a competing event (a cause-specific Cox model). For illustration,
the models are fitted on a random sample of 1500 women and validated on 600
others. The risks by 5 years are given to `nb_val()`.

In `nb_val()`, `predicted_risk =` is a vector or the name of a column of `data`;
`outcome =` is, for a binary outcome, a column name (`"day30"`), a formula
(`~ day30`) or a vector (0/1, logical or a two-level factor), and for a
survival or competing-risks outcome a formula (`~ Surv(years, death)`), a
`Surv` object or the name of a column holding one. The net benefit guide
shows each of them.

```{r data-survival}
rott <- rotterdam
rott$years     <- rott$dtime / 365.25
rott$cr_time   <- ifelse(rott$recur == 1, rott$rtime, rott$dtime) / 365.25
rott$cr_code   <- ifelse(rott$recur == 1, 1, ifelse(rott$death == 1, 2, 0))
rott$cr_status <- factor(rott$cr_code, 0:2, c("censored", "recurrence", "death"))
set.seed(1)
j <- sample(nrow(rott))
df_dev_survival <- rott[j[1:1500], ]
df_val_survival <- rott[j[1501:2100], ]

fit_cox <- coxph(Surv(years, death) ~ age + size + nodes + grade + hormon + chemo,
                 data = df_dev_survival, x = TRUE)
fit_aft <- survreg(Surv(years, death) ~ age + size + nodes, data = df_dev_survival,
                   dist = "weibull")
fit_csc <- riskRegression::CSC(prodlim::Hist(cr_time, cr_code) ~ age + size + nodes + grade,
                               data = df_dev_survival)
# predicted risks by 5 years: of death, and of recurrence (cause 1)
df_val_survival$p_cox <- as.vector(riskRegression::predictRisk(
  fit_cox, newdata = df_val_survival, times = 5))
df_val_survival$p_aft <- as.vector(riskRegression::predictRisk(
  fit_aft, newdata = df_val_survival, times = 5))
df_val_survival$p_csc <- as.vector(riskRegression::predictRisk(
  fit_csc, newdata = df_val_survival, times = 5, cause = 1))

zs <- seq(0.05, 0.60, by = 0.01)
res_surv <- nb_val(data = df_val_survival,
                   predicted_risk = list(Cox = "p_cox", Weibull = "p_aft"),
                   outcome = ~ Surv(years, death),
                   horizon = 5,
                   thresholds = zs)
res_csc <- nb_val(data = df_val_survival,
                  predicted_risk = df_val_survival$p_csc,
                  outcome = ~ Surv(cr_time, cr_status),
                  horizon = 5,
                  cause = "recurrence",
                  thresholds = zs,
                  label = "Cause-specific Cox")

# with conditional IPCW: censoring depends on age, nodes and grade (a Cox
# censoring model, fitted by voipred)
res_ci <- nb_val(data = df_val_survival,
                 predicted_risk = df_val_survival$p_cox,
                 outcome = ~ Surv(years, death),
                 horizon = 5,
                 thresholds = zs,
                 cipcw = ~ age + nodes + grade,
                 label = "Cox")
```

# How the uncertainty is represented

The VoI functions take the result of `nb_val()` and, each time they are
called, draw `n_sim` times (default 1000) from the distribution of the true
net benefit of every strategy given the validation data; all their results
are computed from these draws. The draws are not stored in the result of
`nb_val()`: each function makes them itself, from what `nb_val()` stored (the
predicted risks, the outcomes, the prior). The predicted risks stay fixed;
only the validation sample is uncertain.

How the draws are made depends on the outcome:

| Outcome (in `nb_val()`) | How the draws are made |
|---|---|
| binary, without case weights | from the posterior of the prevalence, sensitivity and specificity (Beta distributions, known in closed form), with the prior given to `nb_val()` |
| survival, competing risks, or binary with case weights | by the Bayesian bootstrap: random weights on the patients (Dirichlet(1, ..., 1)), and the net benefit recomputed with the same estimator as `nb_val()` |

With the default prior, `nb_improper()`, no prior information is used, and
the two ways give the same distribution for a binary outcome: the uncertainty
is that of resampling the patients. (With another prior, such as the
uniform, the prior adds a little information.) For survival and
competing-risks outcomes there is no closed-form posterior of the net benefit
with censored data, so only the default prior is available, and the draws
are the Bayesian bootstrap.

When models are compared, all of them are evaluated on the same patients
within each draw, so their correlation is preserved. With cIPCW the censoring
model is refitted in every draw. `evpi()` computes P(useful) and P(best) from
its own draws (see "EVPI"); with the same seed, models and `n_sim`,
`p_useful()`, `p_best()`, `evpi()` and `evsi()` also use the same draws. This
guide uses `n_sim = 5000`.

**Small effective sample sizes.** When few patients are on one side of a
threshold (typically at very low or very high thresholds), the data say
little there, and the VoI measures can behave unexpectedly; for example,
EVPI may not decrease steadily as the sample size grows (Sadatsafavi et al.,
2023). Interpret them with care at such thresholds. Prior information is one
way to stabilise the estimates (Cruz and Korthauer, 2025; see "The prior" in
the net benefit guide).

The arguments the four functions share:

| Argument | What it does |
|---|---|
| `x`, `...` | Results of `nb_val()`, each with one model or several, for models evaluated on the same data, outcome, thresholds, censoring method and prior. A result with one model given in `...` with a name is labelled with it. For `p_useful()` and `p_best()`, `x` can instead be a result of `evpi()`. |
| `n_sim` | Number of draws. Default 1000. |
| `labels` | Names of the models, one per model, in order. Default: their labels. |

# P(useful)

The probability that a model is better than both default strategies,
$P\{NB_{model} > \max(NB_{all}, 0)\}$: the share of draws in which its net
benefit is strictly higher. It compares each model only with treat all and
treat none, so a model's P(useful) does not depend on the other models; to
compare the models with each other, use `p_best()` (below). Given several
models, `p_useful()` gives P(useful) of each.

```{r pu}
set.seed(10)
pu <- p_useful(res_bin, n_sim = 5000)
```

**`print()`** gives the header (the models, the outcome, the number of
patients, the prior and the number and kind of draws) and P(useful) at the
first thresholds; `print(pu, n = 30)` shows more:

```{r pu-print}
print(pu)
```

**`summary()`** gives, for each model, the thresholds where P(useful) is above
0.95, between 0.5 and 0.95, and below 0.5; with `thresholds`, it also gives
P(useful) at each of them. A P(useful) near 0.5 means that the data give no
evidence either way (the model's net benefit is about that of the best
default strategy), not that the model is likely to be useful:

```{r pu-summary}
summary(pu)
summary(pu, thresholds = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2))
```

**`plot()`** draws P(useful) against the threshold, one curve per model,
named by its label, in the colours of the decision curve (other names with
`labels`, other colours with `colors`):

```{r pu-plot}
plot(pu)
plot(pu, labels = c("Model A", "Model B"), colors = c("darkred", "steelblue"))
```

**Survival** works the same way:

```{r pu-survival}
set.seed(11)
pu_surv <- p_useful(res_surv, n_sim = 5000)
print(pu_surv)
summary(pu_surv)
plot(pu_surv)
```

# P(best)

The probability that each strategy (each model, treat all, treat none) has
the highest net benefit. It compares the models with each other, so
`p_best()` takes the result with all the models. Ties share the draw, so the
probabilities sum to 1 at each threshold.

```{r pb}
set.seed(10)
pb <- p_best(res_bin, n_sim = 5000)
```

**`print()`** gives the header and, at the first thresholds, one column per
strategy:

```{r pb-print}
print(pb)
```

**`summary()`** gives, at each threshold, the strategy most likely to be the
best and its probability (all thresholds by default, or those in
`thresholds`):

```{r pb-summary}
summary(pb, thresholds = c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2))
```

**`plot()`** draws one curve per strategy:

```{r pb-plot}
plot(pb)
```

**Competing risks:**

```{r pb-competing}
set.seed(12)
pb_cr <- p_best(res_csc, n_sim = 5000)
print(pb_cr)
summary(pb_cr, thresholds = c(0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5))
plot(pb_cr)
```

# EVPI

With $ENB_{current} = \max_s E\{NB_s\}$ (use the strategy that is best on
average) and $ENB_{perfect} = E\{\max_s NB_s\}$ (use the best strategy in each
draw), $EVPI = ENB_{perfect} - ENB_{current} \ge 0$: the expected loss in net
benefit from not knowing which strategy is best, in net true positives per
patient. The relative EVPI compares the gain from perfect information with
the gain from using the model(s), both over the best default strategy; 1.2
means perfect information would give 20% more net benefit than using the
best model now.

```{r evpi}
set.seed(10)
e <- evpi(res_bin, n_sim = 5000)
```

**`print()`** gives the header and EVPI and relative EVPI at the first
thresholds:

```{r evpi-print}
print(e)
```

**`summary()`** gives the thresholds where EVPI is positive and its largest
value, and at each threshold EVPI, relative EVPI, the strategy that is best
now (highest expected net benefit) and its expected net benefit (all
thresholds by default, of which the first 10 are printed, or those in
`thresholds`):

```{r evpi-summary}
summary(e, thresholds = c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2))
```

The whole table, `as.data.frame(e)`, also has $ENB_{current}$ and
$ENB_{perfect}$, and `e$ENB` the expected net benefit of each strategy.

**`plot()`** draws EVPI, or the relative EVPI, against the threshold:

```{r evpi-plot}
plot(e)
plot(e, type = "relative")
```

**P(useful) and P(best) from the same draws.** `evpi()` also computes
P(useful) and P(best) from its draws, so the three measures agree with each
other exactly; `p_useful(e)` and `p_best(e)` return them (with no new draws),
with their usual `print()`, `summary()` and `plot()`, and `plot(e, type = )`
draws them. `summary(e)` above has, in the column `P(best)`, the probability
that the strategy that is best now is the best.

```{r evpi-pu-pb}
p_useful(e)
summary(p_best(e), thresholds = c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2))
plot(e, type = "p_useful")
plot(e, type = "p_best")
```

**Several results on one plot**, e.g. the full model alone, validated on 500
and on 2000 patients:

```{r evpi-samples}
res_full <- nb_val(data = df_val_binary,
                   predicted_risk = "p_full",
                   outcome = "day30",
                   thresholds = z,
                   label = "Full")
df_val_binary_2000 <- gusto[i[5001:7000], ]
df_val_binary_2000$p_full <- predict(fit_full, newdata = df_val_binary_2000,
                                     type = "response")
res_full_2000 <- nb_val(data = df_val_binary_2000,
                        predicted_risk = df_val_binary_2000$p_full,
                        outcome = "day30",
                        thresholds = z,
                        label = "Full")
set.seed(10)
e_500  <- evpi(res_full, n_sim = 5000)
e_2000 <- evpi(res_full_2000, n_sim = 5000)
plot(e_500, e_2000, labels = c("n = 500", "n = 2000"))
```

**Survival with cIPCW.** The censoring model is refitted in every draw:
automatically for the Cox model of `cipcw = ~ covariates`, and for your own
censoring model if it is a `coxph`, `survreg`, `rms::cph`, `rms::psm`,
`flexsurvreg` or `prodlim` fit. In a draw where a few patients carry most of the weight,
`coxph()` may warn that a coefficient of the censoring model may be infinite;
one draw out of 5000 has a negligible effect.

```{r evpi-cipcw}
set.seed(41)
e_ci <- evpi(res_ci, n_sim = 5000)
print(e_ci)
summary(e_ci, thresholds = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4))
```

For any other censoring model of your own, give `refit_function` in
`cipcw_control()` (optional, for this case only): a `function(data, weights)`
that refits it with case weights. A survival tree:

```{r evpi-refit}
tree <- partykit::ctree(Surv(years, death == 0) ~ age + nodes + grade,
                        data = df_val_survival)
ctrl <- cipcw_control(
  model = tree,
  refit_function = function(data, weights)
    partykit::ctree(Surv(years, death == 0) ~ age + nodes + grade, data = data,
                    weights = weights))
res_tree <- nb_val(data = df_val_survival,
                   predicted_risk = df_val_survival$p_cox,
                   outcome = ~ Surv(years, death),
                   horizon = 5,
                   thresholds = zs,
                   cipcw = ctrl,
                   label = "Cox")
set.seed(43)
summary(evpi(res_tree, n_sim = 1000), thresholds = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4))
```

**Prior information.** All the results above use the default prior, the
data only. For a binary outcome, prior information can be added in `nb_val()`
(e.g. `prior = nb_uniform()`, see the net benefit guide); the draws then come
from that posterior. Results with different priors are not compared:

```{r evpi-prior}
u_bin <- nb_val(data = df_val_binary,
                predicted_risk = list(Full = "p_full", `Age only` = "p_age"),
                outcome = "day30",
                thresholds = z,
                prior = nb_uniform())
set.seed(30)
summary(evpi(u_bin, n_sim = 5000), thresholds = c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2))
```

# EVSI

The expected gain in net benefit from a future validation study of $N$
patients (`future_n`), added to the current sample, before choosing the
strategy, is quantified by the expected value of sample information (EVSI).
It is between 0 and EVPI and approaches EVPI as $N$ grows. Two
algorithms of Sadatsafavi et al. (2025) are used: the conjugate
(Beta-binomial) one for a binary outcome without case weights, and the
Bayesian bootstrap one otherwise (for survival, a future patient is a
resampled current patient, with the same follow-up).

```{r evsi}
set.seed(20)
o <- evsi(res_bin, future_n = c(250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000), n_sim = 5000)
```

**`print()`** gives the header and, at the first thresholds, EVPI and the
EVSI of each future sample size, one column per size. The prior in the
header is the one given to `nb_val()`. EVPI and EVSI both start from the same
distribution of the true net benefit given the current data (that prior
updated with the validation sample); EVSI then adds the information a future
study of each size would give:

```{r evsi-print}
print(o)
```

**`summary()`** gives EVSI as a percentage of EVPI, at the 3 thresholds with
the largest EVPI (or at chosen `thresholds`): how much of the value of
perfect information a study of each size would give:

```{r evsi-summary}
summary(o)
summary(o, thresholds = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2))
```

**`plot()`** draws EVSI against the future sample size, one curve per
threshold (all thresholds if there are at most 5, otherwise the 4 with the
largest EVPI, or those in `thresholds`), with EVPI as a dashed line:

```{r evsi-plot}
plot(o)
plot(o, thresholds = c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2))
```

Small negative values of EVSI where EVPI is close to 0 are Monte Carlo error:
EVSI is about 0 there.

**Survival:**

```{r evsi-survival}
set.seed(41)
o_s <- evsi(res_surv, future_n = c(500, 1000, 2000, 4000), n_sim = 5000)
print(o_s)
summary(o_s)
plot(o_s, thresholds = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3))
```

# Extracting values

Every result is a list, and its whole table is `as.data.frame()` (the same as
`$estimates`), one row per threshold (and per model, strategy or future
sample size). Thresholds made with `seq()` are not exact decimals (0.1 is
stored as 0.1000000000000000055), so select a threshold with `round()`:

```{r extract}
d_pu <- as.data.frame(pu)
d_pu[round(d_pu$threshold, 2) == 0.1, ]                     # P(useful) at 0.1

d_pb <- as.data.frame(pb)
d_pb[round(d_pb$threshold, 2) == 0.1, ]                     # P(best) at 0.1

d_e <- as.data.frame(e)
d_e$EVPI[round(d_e$threshold, 2) == 0.1]                    # EVPI at 0.1

d_o <- as.data.frame(o)
d_o[round(d_o$threshold, 2) == 0.1 & d_o$future_n == 2000, ]  # EVSI at 0.1, N = 2000
```

# EVPI and EVSI below the decision curve

`plot()` of `nb_val()` results draws EVPI and EVSI in a panel below the decision
curve, on the same threshold axis (without `evpi`, the panel takes the EVPI
of the `evsi()` result):

```{r dca-voi, fig.height = 6.5}
plot(res_bin, evpi = e, evsi = o)
plot(res_bin, type = "delta", evpi = e)
plot(res_surv, evsi = o_s)
```

# Interactive plots

Every plot takes `interactive = TRUE` for a plotly version: hovering shows
the values of all the curves, and clicking a legend entry hides a curve.

```{r interactive, fig.height = 6.5}
plot(pu, interactive = TRUE)
plot(o, thresholds = c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2), interactive = TRUE)
plot(res_bin, evpi = e, evsi = o, interactive = TRUE)
```

# Checks

```{r checks, error = TRUE}
evpi(res_bin, n_sim = 1)                      # at least 2 draws
evpi(res_bin, res_surv)                       # results that cannot be compared
evpi(res_bin, u_bin,                          # different priors
     labels = c("Full", "Age", "Full (uniform)", "Age (uniform)"))
evpi(as.data.frame(res_bin))                  # not a result of nb_val()
evsi(res_bin)                                 # future_n is required
plot(o, thresholds = 0.055)                   # not a threshold of the result
p_useful(res_bin, labels = "a")               # one label per model
plot(res_bin, evpi = pu)                      # evpi = must be a result of evpi()
plot(res_bin, colors = c(Nope = "red"))       # colours named by label
```

# Results computed separately

The models in this guide were given to one call of `nb_val()`. Results
computed separately, for example by different people or at different times,
can be given to the VoI functions together, as long as they come from the
same data, outcome, thresholds and prior (and horizon and censoring):
`evpi(res_a, res_b)`, `p_useful(res_a, res_b)`, `p_best(res_a, res_b)` and
`evsi(res_a, res_b, future_n = ...)`. They are combined (as by `c()`), and the
results are the same as with one call:

```{r separate}
res_full_only <- nb_val(data = df_val_binary, predicted_risk = "p_full",
                        outcome = "day30", thresholds = z, label = "Full")
res_age_only <- nb_val(data = df_val_binary, predicted_risk = "p_age",
                       outcome = "day30", thresholds = z, label = "Age only")
set.seed(50)
e_separate <- evpi(res_full_only, res_age_only)
set.seed(50)
e_one_call <- evpi(res_bin)
all.equal(e_separate$estimates, e_one_call$estimates)
all.equal(p_best(e_separate)$estimates, p_best(e_one_call)$estimates)
```
